The verse gives a short statement with a complete scope: “Surely nothing on earth or in the heavens is hidden from Allah.” It reaches every place a person can see and every place beyond human sight. Nothing in the earth is too small, buried, private, or distant from His knowledge. Nothing in the heavens is too high or remote. The verse follows the warning to people who reject Allah’s revelations and prepares the description of Allah shaping people in the wombs. His knowledge is not limited to public actions or outward form. It includes what is open and what is hidden, what has occurred and what a person cannot reach. This knowledge gives the foundation for guidance and judgment. A human being knows only part of a situation and often discovers what was hidden too late. Allah knows the whole of creation and each person within it. The verse therefore calls the reader to honesty before Allah and trust in His guidance. No secret removes a person from His knowledge, but no need or difficulty is hidden from Him either. The next verse gives one close sign of that knowledge and power in the shaping of every person before birth.

Truly, nothing is hidden from Allah, in the earth or in the heaven He it is Who shapes you in the wombs as He wills. Allah states that He has perfect knowledge in the heavens and earth and that nothing in them is hidden from His watch. He knows everything, whether it is open or hidden. A servant does not breathe a single breath without God counting it muḥṣīhi.

**Earth, heavens, and creation.**

Nothing no existent thing whatever is hidden in heaven and earth from God on account of His knowledge of universals and particulars. God specifies them heaven and earth because sensory perception does not go beyond these. Allah states that He has perfect knowledge in the heavens and earth and that nothing in them is hidden from His watch. Not a particle exists in the heaven and earth unless He is its originator and creator mubdiʿ hi. The right course of action for man can be determined only by a Being who has not only known man from his birth to his death, but also knows what has gone before his birth and what will happen after his death. It is, therefore, only God who, after placing the nature of man in the perspective of the entire universe, may decree what kind of conduct will guarantee man’s success in this world and the next, for a sound human mentality can only be one which is in harmony with the rest of the world and in complete accord with the vaster system of the cosmos.

**Knowledge and guidance.**

Allah states that He has perfect knowledge in the heavens and earth and that nothing in them is hidden from His watch. Only God can truly tell us what He is in His Being and in His attributes. And He has made this so clear in His Book, that any reader who is eager for knowledge of Him will certainly gain enlightenment from it. Again, it is only God who can truly give guidance to man. The right course of action for man can be determined only by a Being who has not only known man from his birth to his death, but also knows what has gone before his birth and what will happen after his death. It is only God who has the power and the knowledge to ordain what it befits human beings to strive for in the present world. This being so, the only realistic approach for man is to trust in His Maker and accept and follow His guidance wholeheartedly and with full confidence.

They are the place to which a reader returns when understanding other passages. “While others are elusive” names verses whose full meaning is not open in the same way. “Those with deviant hearts follow the elusive verses seeking ˹to spread˺ doubt through their ˹false˺ interpretations” describes a wrong approach: leaving the clear foundation and using an elusive expression to create confusion. “But none grasps their ˹full˺ meaning except Allah” sets a limit around what a person can claim to know. “As for those well-grounded in knowledge, they say, ‘We believe in this ˹Quran˺—it is all from our Lord’” gives the response of people firmly grounded in knowledge. They do not divide the Book against itself or use one part to deny another. “But none will be mindful ˹of this˺ except people of reason” closes by asking for an attentive mind. The verse does not make the unclear a reason to ignore the Quran. It gives the clear verses their central place, directs the reader away from false interpretation, and teaches faith and humility before what Allah has kept fully within His knowledge. The distinction between the two kinds of verses protects the reader from two errors. One is to ignore the clear foundation of the Book while chasing an expression that can be bent toward a desired claim. The other is to assume that faith means pretending to know every unseen reality in full. The verse gives another way: clear verses guide belief and action, elusive verses are received with faith, and all of the Book is known to come from the same Lord. This makes knowledge a source of humility rather than a tool for spreading doubt. A reader can study, reflect, and seek the best understanding without turning limited human language into a claim to possess what Allah has kept within His own full knowledge. People of reason do not set one part of the Quran against another. They allow what is clear to provide the firm basis, and they respond to what is elusive with faith in Allah and care in interpretation. This is the discipline of knowledge: trust the Book, use its clear foundation, and leave full knowledge of what is hidden to Allah.

The warning is placed within a history of repeated human response to Allah’s signs. “Their fate will be like that of the people of Pharaoh and those before them” points to peoples whose power did not keep them from the result of their wrongdoing. Pharaoh’s people are not named here as distant history for curiosity. They are an example of a pattern: authority, numbers, and outward strength do not cancel accountability before Allah. “They all rejected Our signs” identifies the central wrong. The issue is not simply that they faced hardship or lost a contest of power; they denied what Allah had shown them. “So Allah seized them for their sins” connects the consequence to their own rejection and wrongdoing. “And Allah is severe in punishment” closes the verse with a warning that His judgment is real and not an empty threat. It follows the statement that wealth and children cannot benefit disbelievers against Allah, then shows the same truth in the fate of earlier communities. The reader is invited to learn from history before being forced to learn from loss: signs are sent for recognition and response, not for denial. The phrase “their fate will be like that of the people of Pharaoh and those before them” also keeps the warning from being read as a story about someone else alone. It puts present hearers within a pattern that can recur whenever people receive signs and then reject them. To call Allah “severe in punishment” is therefore to take His warning seriously, while still recognising that the signs themselves came as guidance before judgment.

**People of Pharaoh and those before them.**

Their way is as the way as the habit of Pharaoh’s folk and the communities of people before them such as ‘Ād and Thamūd who denied Our signs; God seized them He destroyed them for their sins this statement explains the previous one; God is severe in retribution. Other scholars said that the Ayah means, "Like the practice, conduct, likeness of the people of Fir'awn. 13.text:
The verse gives a visible event as a sign for reflection. “Indeed, there was a sign for you in the two armies that met in battle” directs attention to two groups that faced one another at Badr. “One fighting for the cause of Allah and the other in denial” distinguishes them by what they stood for, not merely by their numbers. The believers “saw their enemy twice their number,” so the scene did not give them an ordinary worldly reason to feel secure. “But Allah supports with His victory whoever He wills” explains why numbers alone cannot tell the whole story. Help and victory belong to Allah, and He gives support as He wills. “Surely in this is a lesson for people of insight” asks the reader to see more than a military report. The event teaches that truth is not measured by visible resources and that apparent weakness does not place believers outside Allah’s support. It follows the warning to those who opposed the Prophet and gives an example connected to that warning. The lesson is not a promise that effort, planning, patience, and moral responsibility no longer matter. It corrects the belief that power belongs permanently to whoever has more people, wealth, or equipment. The meeting has a moral difference: faith and denial are not understood only by who appears to win. People of insight learn from the sign without making numbers their lord. They see that Allah can support a small group, humble a larger group, and make an event a warning as well as a victory. The sign therefore speaks to people who face an imbalance of resources and are tempted to think that visible force decides every matter. It gives neither side permission for pride. Believers are directed toward trust, steadfastness, and the cause of Allah; those who deny are warned that numbers and equipment cannot make falsehood secure. The lesson belongs to insight because it asks the reader to look beneath an immediate result to Allah’s power, promise, and wisdom. It also joins the event to the verses before it: those who reject guidance may look strong for a time, yet Allah can make their strength fail and make support clear for those who rely on Him. The verse turns a historical meeting into a continuing call to recognise where real help comes from.

**The two armies at Badr.**

There has already been a sign an example the verb qad kāna ‘there has been’ is used to separate the statement to follow from the previous one for you in two hosts two parties that met one another in battle on the day of Badr; one company fighting in the way of God in obedience to Him namely the Prophet and his Companions who numbered three hundred and thirteen men most of them on foot with two horses six plates of armour and eight swords; and another unbelieving; they the disbelievers numbering almost a thousand saw them the Muslims twice the like of them that is more numerous than themselves as the eye sees in manifest vision witnessing; and God granted them victory despite their fewer number; for God confirms He strengthens with His help whom He will granting him victory. In the previous verses, the disbelievers were informed that they will be overcome. Now, cited in this verse is an example of how the prophecy has been fulfilled. This verse refers to the Battle of Badr in which the disbelievers had about 1000 men, 700 camels and 100 horses, while the Muslim mujahidin were just over 300, having a total of 70 camels, 2 horses, 6 armours and 8 swords. Threatening the Jews With Defeat and Encouraging Them to Learn a Lesson From the Battle of Badr. Muhammad bin Ishaq bin Yasar recorded that 'Asim bin 'Umar bin Qatadah said that when the Messenger of Allah gained victory in the battle of Badr and went back to Al-Madīnah, he gathered the Jews in the marketplace of Bani Qaynuqa'. (There was a token) a sign confirming the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ (for you) O people of Makkah (in two hosts) in two groups: that of Muhammad and that of Abu Sufyan (which met) on the Day of Badr: You had a sign for the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ in the form of two groups-that of Muhammad and that of Abu Sufyan-who met on the Day of Badr. There has already been a sign for you in two hosts that met; one com pany fighting in the way of God; and another unbelieving; they saw them twice the like of them; for God confirms with His help whom He will.

**Numbers and what was seen.**

There has already been a sign an example the verb qad kāna ‘there has been’ is used to separate the statement to follow from the previous one for you in two hosts two parties that met one another in battle on the day of Badr; one company fighting in the way of God in obedience to Him namely the Prophet and his Companions who numbered three hundred and thirteen men most of them on foot with two horses six plates of armour and eight swords; and another unbelieving; they the disbelievers numbering almost a thousand saw them the Muslims twice the like of them that is more numerous than themselves as the eye sees in manifest vision witnessing; and God granted them victory despite their fewer number; for God confirms He strengthens with His help whom He will granting him victory. The encounter was certainly strange as each combating group saw the opponent being twice its own numbers. The sighting of so many Muslims inspired awe in the hearts of the disbelievers, while Muslims who saw the disbelievers as twice of them turned to Allah more fervently. If the actual number of disbelievers which was three times more than their own were to be realized by Muslims, they may have been overawed. This state of sighting the numbers of the other group as twice its own was at a particular time. At another time each of the two combating groups felt the other one as low in numbers, as it would appear later in Surah al-Anfal. (They saw them with their own eyes twice their number) means, the idolators thought that the Muslims were twice as many as they were, for Allah made this illusion a factor in the victory that Islam had over them. (They saw them with their own eyes twice their number) is that the Muslims saw twice as many idolators as they were, yet Allah gave them victory over the disbelievers. 'Abdullah bin Mas'ud said, "When we looked at the disbelievers' forces, we found that they were twice as many as we were. When the two camps saw each other, the Muslims thought that the idolators were twice as many as they were, so that they would trust in Allah and seek His help. Abu Sufyan and his army which consisted of 950 men, (whom they saw) they saw themselves (as twice their number) as twice the number as that of the Companions of Muhammad ﷺ (clearly, with their very eyes). The believers actually saw the disbelievers as being double their real number; but Allah helped His allies. When God wants an affair to be accomplished He makes many appear to be few in the eyes of one people and few to appear as many in the eyes of another people.

**Allah’s help and victory.**

There has already been a sign an example the verb qad kāna ‘there has been’ is used to separate the statement to follow from the previous one for you in two hosts two parties that met one another in battle on the day of Badr; one company fighting in the way of God in obedience to Him namely the Prophet and his Companions who numbered three hundred and thirteen men most of them on foot with two horses six plates of armour and eight swords; and another unbelieving; they the disbelievers numbering almost a thousand saw them the Muslims twice the like of them that is more numerous than themselves as the eye sees in manifest vision witnessing; and God granted them victory despite their fewer number; for God confirms He strengthens with His help whom He will granting him victory. They had hopes of Allah's help, and ultimate victory, because they had placed their total trust in Allah, were steadfast and sincerely believed in the promise of Allah revealed to them in the following words: To sum up, it can be safely said that making a small group of people with very little to fight against a much stronger group and score a victory, as prophesied in Makkah, is an unusual event full of lessons for the observant and the discerning. You have an Ayah, meaning proof, that Allah will make His religion prevail, award victory to His Messenger, make His Word apparent and His religion the highest. (so that Allah might accomplish a matter already ordained.)[8:42] meaning, so that the truth and falsehood are distinguishable, and thus the word of faith prevails over disbelief and deviation, so that the believers prevail and the disbelievers are humiliated. In spite of this, those who denied the truth suffered a crushing defeat and the believers achieved a decisive victory. This is a clear proof that God is always on the side of the believers. In the face of such a great difference in resources, an extraordinary victory cannot be achieved without God’s succour. This serves as a demonstration from God that truth does not go unsupported. (Thus Allah strengtheneth with His succour whom He will) i.e. Allah gives His support to whomever He wishes.

**A lesson for people of insight.**

Surely in that which is mentioned is a lesson for people of vision those who are discerning so will you not be warned by this and become believers? To sum up, it can be safely said that making a small group of people with very little to fight against a much stronger group and score a victory, as prophesied in Makkah, is an unusual event full of lessons for the observant and the discerning. This serves as a demonstration from God that truth does not go unsupported. It is also a clear indication to those who deny the truth of how they are placed in this world. There are obvious signs in the words and deeds of the preacher that the Truth he preaches comes from God. But the arrogant find refuge in fine words to refute this. They live by false explanations, until finally they leave for the next world, only to learn that the words in which they had taken refuge were utterly meaningless from the standpoint of reality. (Lo! Herein) in Allah enabling Muhammad to triumph on the Day of Badr (verily is a lesson for those who have eyes) concerning Religion, i.e. the believers; it is also said that this means: it was a lesson for those who saw it with their own eyes. In that there is a lesson and a warning for those of insight to realize that the help of Allah can come to the believers even though they may be few in number; and that defeat can come to those on falsehood even though they may be great in number. If He covers the inner sight baṣīra of a people the sharpness of their physical eyes abṣār will not benefit them.

14.text:
The verse names things people naturally desire and puts them in their proper place. “The enjoyment of ˹worldly˺ desires—women, children, treasures of gold and silver, fine horses, cattle, and fertile land” introduces attractions that can fill a person’s attention. These are not all described as evil in themselves. Family, wealth, animals, and land can serve real needs and support human life. The warning lies in treating their attraction as the highest good and forgetting why they were given. “Has been made appealing to people” acknowledges the strength of this pull and the reality of a test. “These are the pleasures of this worldly life” gives them their limit: they belong to a passing life and cannot provide the final destination of the human being. “But with Allah is the finest destination” directs desire beyond what fades, toward the return Allah has prepared. The following verse immediately asks whether the reader should be told of something better than these attractions. Together, the verses do not command a person to deny every lawful comfort. They teach the heart not to become captive to comforts, possessions, status, or the future of one’s family while losing sight of Allah and the lasting home with Him. The list also shows why the test can be difficult. Its objects are familiar and tangible, and some are connected with care, work, dignity, or survival. The verse does not pretend that their appeal is unreal. Instead, it teaches the reader to recognise their passing character and to keep the finest destination in view when making choices about money, family, land, and comfort. A person can therefore possess and care for these things without giving them the place that belongs to Allah. The question is not whether the world has beauty, but whether its beauty makes the servant forget the Lord, the return, and the life that does not perish. Keeping the finest destination in sight gives worldly work, wealth, and family their proper measure. It lets the gifts serve faith instead of becoming a barrier to it. The person who remembers Allah can enjoy a lawful gift with gratitude and use it for a good purpose, while knowing that it cannot remain forever. The heart is protected when it treats the world as a place of work and trial rather than the home for which every desire must be spent.

**Worldly desires and their attraction.**

Beautified for mankind is love of lusts that which the self lusts after and calls for beautified by Satan or by God as a test — of women children stored-up heaps of gold and silver horses of mark fine horses cattle namely camels cows and sheep and tillage the cultivation of land. The first verse here names some of the most de-sired things and says that they have been made to look attractive and therefore, people go after them enticed by their glamour brushing aside any concerns for the life to come, if there be any. Then come other forms of wealth and possessions - gold, silver, cattle and tillage - which attract people secondarily. Why has man been made in a way that he is temperamentally attracted to these things? Beautified for men is the love of things they covet; women, children, Qanatir Al-Muqantarah of gold and silver, branded beautiful horses (Musawwamah), cattle and fertile land. Allah mentions the delights that He put in this life for people, such as women and children, and He started with women, because the test with them is more tempting. (Beautified for mankind is) what people's hearts find desirable is (love of the joys (that come) from women) meaning slave women and wives (and offspring) slaves and children, (and stored up heaps) amassed wealth (of gold and silver) it is also said that this means: minted or engraved gold and silver, (and horses branded (with their mark) beautiful branded horses and grazing in pastures, (and cattle) i.e. sheep, cows and camels (and land) cultivation and cultivated lands. Allah tells us that He has made the love of desirable things of this world attractive to people in order to test them. These desirable things include women, children, wealth (in the form of gold and silver) that is overflowing and piled up, beautiful trained horses, livestock (such as camels, cows and sheep), as well as farmlands – all of which is the enjoyment of the life of the world which lasts only for a short while. Adorned for people is love of appetites, like women, children, heaped-up heaps of gold and silver, horses of mark, cattle, and tillage.

**A test and a purpose.**

Why has man been made in a way that he is temperamentally attracted to these things? If man was not naturally inclined to and even enamoured with these things, all worldly business would have gone topsy-turvy. If we think about it, we shall realize that it was the love for what is desirable in this mortal world which brought them out of their homes, and in this silent process, gave the world a strong and ongoing social system. However, as for verses where such glamorization of things has been attributed to Satan - for example, (the Satan has made their deeds look attractive to them - 8:48; 16:63; 27:24; 29:38.) - there the reference is to things that are evil, religiously and rationally; or, the reference is to a false sense of adornment which is evil because it transgresses the limits set by Allah: Similarly, man's wealth and possessions are means of convenience for his role in this world and in the life to come - provided that they do not enter into his heart, sit there, and kill it in the process. In other words, it means that all these things are there simply to serve a purpose in man's mortal life in the present world and certainly not to have him fall in love with things for their own sake, for the real beauty of the experience lies in one's ultimate resort with Allah in blissful eternity enjoying what would never perish, diminish or weaken. God, wishing to ascertain which of His creatures are capable of rising above worldly attractions, has so willed it that man should be attracted to and find gratification in the things of this world, but at the same time be faced with the choice of clinging to them or renouncing them in favour of the unseen things of the next world. This is not an easy choice, for he sees that worldly acquisitions lead him to an honourable place in society. This presents the greatest obstacle to advancing towards the demands of the Hereafter. Allah tells us that He has made the love of desirable things of this world attractive to people in order to test them.

**Wealth, family, and worldly life.**

The reason for this and for all evil deeds is, in fact, the love of the worldly life. It means that the love of dunya (worldly life or worldly enjoyments) is the main source of all errors. He enjoys the blessings of the present life and uses its means for success in the life to come. Similarly, man's wealth and possessions are means of convenience for his role in this world and in the life to come - provided that they do not enter into his heart, sit there, and kill it in the process. When the purpose for having children is to reproduce and increase the Ummah of Muhammad with those who worship Allah alone without partners, then it is encouraged and praised. Sometimes, owners of horses collect them to be used in the cause of Allah, and when warranted, they use their horses in battle. Another type collects horses to boast, and out of enmity to the people of Islam, and this type earns a burden for his behavior. Another type collects horses to fulfill their needs and to collect their offspring, and they do not forget Allah's right due on their horses. All his interests and activities centre around his family, his wealth and his property. He is so engrossed in building the future of his children in this world, that he no longer remembers the fact that there is any ‘future’ beyond this present life, to which he should give thought. Providing all comforts for his home in this world becomes so dear to him that it never occurs to him that there is any other home save this, to which he should pay heed. Making money, accumulating riches and possessing property in this world seem so estimable to him, that he fails to realize that there is any ‘wealth’ other than this, to which he should devote his life.

**The excellent abode.**

That which is mentioned is the comfort of the life of this world enjoyed while it lasts but then perishes; but God — with Him is the more excellent abode place of return which is Paradise and for this reason one should desire none other than this abode. This is the pleasure of the present world's life; but Allah has the excellent return with Him Say: (But Allah has the excellent return with Him) meaning, the best destination and reward. This Ayah means, "Say, O Muhammad, to the people, 'Should I tell you about what is better than the delights and joys of this life that will soon perish?'" Allah informed them of what is better when He said,. (That) which is mentioned above (is comfort of the life of the world) is of benefit to people in the life of this world and then it vanishes; it is also said that this means: the joys of this world last only for as long as the stuff of any home, a bowl, a plate and the like. (Allah! With Him is a more excellent abode) in the Hereafter, i.e. A believer should not become attached to these things as Allah has kept the best place of return for him: the Paradise that is as wide as the heavens and the earth. However, all these things with the external glitter of this present life will be of no use to him in the next, eternal life. It is only one who makes the permanent life of the Hereafter the focus of his attention who will realize the insignificance of these worldly things. " Gabriel went and saw those adorned paradises with their infinite joy and bliss, that place of revelry made and prepared in the neighborhood of God's Presence for the exalted ones of the road and God's friends. When Gabriel came back he said, "Lord God, 'By Thy exaltedness, no one will hear of it and not enter into it!' By the exaltedness of Your Lordhood, no one will hear the attributes of this para dise without aiming for it and becoming obedient so that he may enter it. " Then the Lord of the Worlds surrounded paradise with all the hardship and suffering of unwor thy things and unreached desires, and He made its road a bridge of trial so that everyone who aims for the Patron must first pass over that bridge of trial.

15.text:
The verse answers the previous list of worldly attractions by showing what is better. “Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ ‘Shall I inform you of what is better than ˹all of˺ this?’” invites the reader to compare what passes with what Allah has prepared. “Those mindful ˹of Allah˺ will have Gardens with their Lord under which rivers flow” places the promise with people who keep Allah in view and shape their actions around Him. “to stay there forever” names a home of abundance and permanence, unlike comforts that can disappear during this life. “And pure spouses” brings companionship free from the harms and imperfections that trouble worldly relationships. “Along with Allah’s pleasure” names a gift greater than material delight: Allah’s approval of His servants. “And Allah is All-Seeing of ˹His˺ servants” closes by assuring that the Lord who promises this reward sees their faith, their choices, and their work. The verse does not ask a person to despise the gifts named before it. It changes the scale by which they are weighed. Worldly pleasures are temporary; the return with Allah is lasting. The next verses describe the people who seek that return through faith, forgiveness, patience, truthfulness, obedience, generosity, and prayer. The comparison is an invitation to choose the better object of hope and to see every blessing in light of the One who gives it. The promised Gardens, the flowing rivers, pure companionship, and Allah’s pleasure give the reader a complete picture of a return that is better than passing delight. This hope does not make present responsibilities unimportant. It gives them a lasting direction, because Allah sees His servants and knows the faith, patience, and obedience with which they turn toward Him. The person who seeks His pleasure does not lose the good of this life; that person learns to receive it without making it the final goal.

**Better than worldly pleasures.**

Say O Muhammad to your people ‘Shall I tell you shall I inform you of something better than that? that which has been mentioned of lusts this interrogative is meant as an affirmative. Here, the address is to the Holy Prophet who is being asked to tell those who become obsessed with imperfect and perishable blessings they find in the present life that he is in a position to lead them on to far better blessings. This is the pleasure of the present world's life; but Allah has the excellent return with Him Say: This Ayah means, "Say, O Muhammad, to the people, 'Should I tell you about what is better than the delights and joys of this life that will soon perish?'" Allah informed them of what is better when He said,. Shall I tell you about something better than those desirable things? Shall I tell you of something better than that? After talking about the enemies, describing their life, and explaining their furthest goal, God in this verse comes back to the story of the friends.

**Gardens and lasting blessings.**

For those that are fearful of idolatry with their Lord ‘inda rabbihim is the predicate the subject being the following jannātun…’ are Gardens underneath which rivers flow abiding therein decreed for them therein is eternal life when they enter it and spouses purified of menstruation and other impurities and beatitude read ridwān or rudwān meaning ‘much pleasure’ from God; and God is Seer knower of His servants requiting each of them according to his deeds. For those who fear Allah, there are with their Lord gardens beneath which rivers flow, where they shall live forever, and wives purified, and approval from Allah. These shall be the lot of those who fear Allah and are obedient to Him. As compared to that, only three blessings of the Hereafter, that is, the gardens of Par-adise, wives purified and the approval from Allah have been identified. (For those who keep from evil) keep from disbelief, ascribing partners to Allah and indecencies, in reference to Abu Bakr and his fellow believers, (with their Lord, are Gardens beneath which) beneath its trees and habitations (rivers) of wine, honey, milk and water (flow, wherein they will abide for ever) they will dwell in Paradise: they shall neither die nor leave it (and pure companions) they have therein spouses who are spared menses and filth, (and contentment from Allah) and the contentment of Allah is far greater than the bliss they enjoy. Those who are mindful of Allah by fulfilling His commands and avoiding His prohibitions will have gardens with trees and palaces overlooking flowing streams in which they will live eternally. They will also have wives who will be free from any defects in their form or character. Tomorrow, the final outcome of those whose watch word today is godwariness will be paradise and approval. The first degree is the Garden of the Shelter, and the first level of godwariness is to avoid the forbidden and the soul's caprice.

**Allah’s pleasure and His servants.**

The verse describes how the prayer of faith appears in a person’s life. “It is they who are patient, sincere, obedient, and charitable” gives a connected account of a life shaped by faith. Patience is steady endurance in obedience, in leaving wrongdoing, and in trials that are not chosen. Sincerity points to truthfulness in faith and conduct, so that a person’s words are not separated from what they do. Obedience describes willing submission to Allah rather than treating faith as a claim without action. Charity turns this inward faith outward through giving from what Allah has provided. “And who pray for forgiveness before dawn” shows that they return to Allah in the quiet last part of the night, asking pardon rather than becoming satisfied with their deeds. The qualities are linked, not separate labels. Patience keeps a person from giving up; truthfulness keeps faith real; obedience directs the life; generosity serves others; and seeking forgiveness keeps the servant humble before Allah. The verse completes the description of those who will receive the better return named before it. Their hope for Paradise and Allah’s pleasure is joined to a life of devotion, service, and repeated repentance. This return for pardon gives every virtue its proper place: the servant continues to need Allah’s mercy while seeking His pleasure. The virtues also form a pattern that reaches both private and public life. Patience meets difficulty, sincerity guards the heart, obedience gives direction, charity reaches those in need, and forgiveness before dawn keeps the servant near Allah. This is not a list for admiration alone. It gives a way for faith to be lived with steadiness, humility, generosity, and hope until the return to Allah. This pattern is also a protection against pride. A person may have patience, speak truth, obey, and give, yet still need to ask forgiveness. The early prayer returns every good deed to Allah’s mercy and keeps the heart from thinking that its own effort is enough. In this way, service to people and worship of Allah remain joined in one life.
